What exactly is an enzyme?

blocks.x: An enzyme is a biocatalyst made by living cells — mostly protein in nature (with a rare exception: some RNA molecules called ribozymes can act as enzymes too). Enzymes are colloidal and thermolabile, meaning they're heat-sensitive, and each one is highly specific in what it does.

Slide 5 of the original lecture put it perfectly: an enzyme and its substrate are like a teacher and a student. The teacher (enzyme) helps the student (substrate) transform — understanding a topic, passing an exam — but the teacher themself doesn't fundamentally change in the process and remains available to help the next student. Enzymes work the same way: they speed up a reaction and are released unchanged, ready to catalyze the same reaction again and again.

Key characteristics: when a substrate binds an enzyme, product is released; the enzyme loses activity if denatured (its shape disrupted); many enzymes need helper molecules called cofactors; and all of them dramatically accelerate the making and breaking of chemical bonds.

sections.title: Why is an enzyme called what it's called?

blocks.x: Early enzymes were named arbitrarily by whoever discovered them — names like pepsin, trypsin, and chymotrypsin tell you nothing about their function. Later, the suffix "-ase" was tacked onto the substrate name instead — lipase acts on lipids, lactase on lactose, nuclease on nucleic acids. These are called trivial names, and they still don't tell the full story.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — nicknames vs. official job titles

blocks.x: It's like calling someone "Auntie Ama the seller" instead of giving her an official job title that describes exactly what she does, for whom, and how. In 1961, the International Union of Biochemistry (IUB) set up an Enzyme Commission to fix this — giving every enzyme a proper "job title" under a systematic classification.
Since 1964, enzymes have been sorted into six major classes by the type of reaction they perform:

blocks.x: Oxidoreductases handle oxidation-reduction reactions — like an electrician moving current from one wire to another. Transferases move a functional group from one molecule to the next — like a Mobile Money agent transferring credit from one account to another.

Hydrolases break bonds using water — like soaking dried gari in water to soften and break it apart. Lyases add or remove small groups (water, ammonia, CO₂) without using water in a hydrolysis step — like squeezing an orange to remove juice without soaking it first.

Isomerases just rearrange atoms already present — like reshaping the same lump of banku dough into a different form. Ligases join two molecules together, spending ATP to do it — like a welder fusing two metal rods, and the ATP is the "gas" that powers the welding torch.

sections.title: How big is an enzyme, and where does the action happen?

blocks.x: Enzymes are generally globular (globe-shaped) proteins, ranging from about 62 to over 2,500 amino acids in size — usually much bigger than the substrates they work on. Yet only a tiny portion, around 2–6 amino acids, is directly involved in catalysis. This tiny working region is called the active site.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a whole factory building for one small workbench

blocks.x: Picture a huge factory building, but all the actual assembly happens at one small workbench inside it — the rest of the building exists just to support and position that workbench correctly. That's an enzyme: a large protein whose real business happens at a small pocket, cleft, or crevice — the active site — where the substrate binds.

blocks.x: Active sites aren't rigid boxes — they're flexible clefts, commonly built from amino acids like serine (the most frequent), aspartate, histidine, cysteine, lysine, arginine, glutamate, and tyrosine. Each enzyme's unique amino acid sequence folds into a unique 3D shape with unique properties — and that same folding can be undone. Heat or chemical denaturants can denature an enzyme, unfolding it and destroying its activity — sometimes reversibly, sometimes permanently.

sections.title: Why can't just any enzyme act on any molecule?

blocks.x: Enzymes are usually very picky — specificity mostly comes down to matching shape and charge between enzyme and substrate.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a SIM card only fitting its own tray

blocks.x: Just as a SIM card only fits into the SIM tray shaped and sized for it, an enzyme's active site is molded to fit only substrates with the right shape and the right electrical charge pattern. Force the wrong SIM in and nothing happens — same with the wrong substrate.

This specificity is exactly why enzymes can carry out such an enormous range of essential jobs: powering respiration, digestion, muscle and nerve function, blood coagulation, healing, and more. Even some surprising jobs — firefly luciferase, for example, is the enzyme responsible for the glowing light of fireflies and click beetles.

sections.title: How does an enzyme actually "grip" its substrate?

blocks.x: Two competing models have tried to explain this over the years.

The very first model proposed. It assumes the enzyme's active site is rigid and pre-shaped — the substrate simply fits into it "just as a key fits into the proper lock." Analogy: a padlock that only opens with one specific, unbending key. The problem: this model can't explain the effects of allosteric modulators or many real enzymatic behaviors, since it assumes nothing ever flexes.

A refinement: the active site is NOT rigid — it's continuously reshaped as the substrate approaches, molding itself to achieve a precise fit. Analogy: pulling on a rubber glove — the glove isn't a fixed hand-shape sitting there waiting; it flexes and moulds itself around your hand as you put it on. This model successfully explains competitive inhibition and allosteric effects.

sections.title: Cofactors, Coenzymes & Prosthetic Groups

blocks.x: Some enzymes work perfectly well alone. Others need extra, non-protein "helper molecules" called <term d="Non-protein chemical compounds that bind to an enzyme and assist it in catalyzing a reaction.">cofactors</term> to function at all — either organic or inorganic, and classified by how tightly they bind.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — staff on contract vs. staff on payroll

blocks.x: A coenzyme is like a casual contract worker — loosely attached, coming and going, ferrying materials from one job site (enzyme) to another. A prosthetic group is like a permanent staff member — tightly, stably built into the "company" (the enzyme) by strong covalent or noncovalent bonds, always there. When the helper is present, you have a fully staffed holoenzyme (enzyme + cofactor). Remove the helper, and you're left with just the empty shell — the apoenzyme.

e.g. pyridoxal phosphate, FMN, FAD, thiamine pyrophosphate, biotin, and metal ions like Co, Cu, Mg, Mn, Se, and Zn (found in <term d="Enzymes that require a bound metal ion for their catalytic activity.">metalloenzymes</term>).
Organic examples: Thiamin, Riboflavin, Niacin, Biotin. Inorganic examples: Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺, Zn²⁺, Mn²⁺. Coenzymes shuttle chemical groups between different enzymes in a pathway.

sections.title: What speeds an enzyme up — or shuts it down?

blocks.x: As temperature rises, enzyme activity usually rises too — up to a point. Push it too far, and just like an egg turning solid in a hot pan, the protein denatures and can't return to its working shape. This is exactly why refrigeration preserves food (it slows down spoilage-causing bacterial enzymes), and why doctors sometimes deliberately lower a patient's body temperature (induced hypothermia) during certain surgeries to slow the metabolic rate.

blocks.title: pH — like a fish needing the right water

blocks.x: Every enzyme has an optimum pH where it works fastest. Move too far above or below that point, and activity drops sharply — at extreme pH, the enzyme becomes completely inactive. It's like a freshwater fish suddenly placed in the sea — the wrong environment simply doesn't work, no matter how much food (substrate) is available.

blocks.x: Low substrate means most active sites sit empty — few collisions, slow reaction. As substrate rises, more collisions occur and the rate climbs — until active sites are almost continuously full. Beyond that point, adding more substrate doesn't speed things up further; the rate levels off. Analogy: like a market stall with a fixed number of sales counters — once every counter has a customer, adding more customers to the queue doesn't sell goods any faster.

Too little enzyme, and there aren't enough "workers" to process all the substrate — the reaction lags. Add more enzyme, and the rate increases (as long as substrate is plentiful). Analogy: adding more cashiers at a busy bank speeds up service — but only if there are still enough customers waiting to serve.

UV, beta, gamma, and X-rays can inactivate enzymes by generating damaging peroxides — for example, UV rays inhibit salivary amylase. Analogy: like leaving black cloth out in strong sun for too long — the sun's energy degrades and damages the material over time.
Putting numbers on it — Michaelis–Menten kinetics

Raising substrate concentration speeds an enzyme up, but not forever. Plot rate against substrate concentration and you get a curve that rises steeply, then flattens into a plateau. That plateau is the enzyme working flat out, with every active site occupied.
v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]) — the Michaelis–Menten equation, which describes that curve.

The maximum rate the enzyme can reach when it is saturated with substrate. Adding more substrate past this point changes nothing — every active site is already busy. Vmax depends on how much enzyme is present.

The substrate concentration at which the enzyme runs at half of Vmax. Read it backwards: a low Km means the enzyme reaches half speed on very little substrate, so it has high affinity. A high Km means low affinity. Km is a property of the enzyme itself and does not change with enzyme concentration.
How many substrate molecules one enzyme molecule converts per second when saturated. Carbonic anhydrase is among the fastest known, at roughly a million per second.

blocks.title: Where you have already met K<sub>m</sub> without realising

blocks.x: Hexokinase (muscle, brain) has a low Km — it grabs glucose even when blood sugar is low, so those tissues never go short. Glucokinase (liver) has a high Km — it only works hard after a meal, when glucose is plentiful, which is exactly what an organ that mops up excess sugar should do. Same reaction, different Km, completely different job.

blocks.title: Not every enzyme follows this curve

blocks.x: Allosteric enzymes give an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve instead of the usual hyperbola, because their subunits show cooperativity — one subunit binding substrate makes the next bind more easily. Such enzymes do not obey Michaelis–Menten kinetics, so quoting a simple Km for them is wrong. The familiar example of cooperative binding is haemoglobin binding oxygen (a transport protein, not an enzyme), and phosphofructokinase-1 in glycolysis behaves the same way.

sections.title: What happens when something jams the machine?

blocks.x: An enzyme inhibitor is anything that binds an enzyme and reduces its activity. Inhibition comes in two broad flavours: reversible and irreversible.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — different ways to jam an ATM

blocks.x: Think of the enzyme as an ATM machine designed to process one specific card. Different inhibitors interfere in different ways:

The inhibitor closely resembles the real substrate (a substrate analogue) and competes directly for the active site. As long as it's sitting there, the real substrate can't bind. Analogy: someone using a fake, similar-looking card to occupy the ATM's card slot — as long as their fake card is inserted, your real card simply can't go in.

The inhibitor binds a completely different site (an allosteric site), changing the enzyme's shape and impairing function — with no structural resemblance to the substrate at all. It can bind the free enzyme. Analogy: someone jams the ATM's internal control panel — your card still fits the slot fine, but the machine itself is broken and can't process anything.

Binds ONLY the enzyme-substrate complex — never the free enzyme — usually at an allosteric site, causing a shape change. Analogy: the ATM only jams once your card is already inside and a transaction is in progress — it clamps down mid-process.
Can bind either the free enzyme (competitive-like) or the enzyme-substrate complex (uncompetitive-like) — a hybrid of both behaviours.

blocks.cap: Four ways a reversible inhibitor can interfere — each targeting a different point in the enzyme's cycle.

blocks.x: Because reversible inhibitors bind non-covalently, removing the inhibitor restores full activity. This gives cells a fast, dynamic way to turn pathways up or down as metabolic needs change — essential for maintaining homeostasis.
Here, the inhibitor binds covalently and permanently inactivates the enzyme — like pouring superglue into the ATM's card slot; it's not coming back online. These are usually toxic substances:

items: Organophosphorus insecticides (and related nerve agents) block acetylcholine esterase, an enzyme essential for nerve conduction, causing paralysis of vital body functions.
Certain antibiotics irreversibly inhibit serine-containing enzymes involved in bacterial cell wall synthesis.

Disulfiram (Antabuse®), used to treat alcoholism, irreversibly inhibits acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, causing acetaldehyde to build up — producing the unpleasant flushing, headache, nausea, and anxiety that discourage drinking.

blocks.x: Telling inhibitors apart — the Lineweaver–Burk plot

The Michaelis–Menten curve flattens gradually, which makes Vmax hard to read off accurately by eye. The Lineweaver–Burk plot (also called the double-reciprocal plot) fixes that by plotting 1/v against 1/[S], which turns the curve into a straight line.

Because each inhibitor changes K<sub>m</sub> and V<sub>max</sub> differently, each produces a distinctive pattern of lines — which is exactly why exam questions show you a graph and ask what kind of inhibition it is:

c: Lines meet on the y-axis (same y-intercept), slope steeper
A separate site, enzyme or ES
Lines meet on the x-axis (same x-intercept), y-intercept higher

blocks.title: The fastest way to remember it

blocks.x: Competitive fights the substrate for the same seat — so flooding the system with substrate wins, and the enzyme can still reach full speed (Vmax unchanged), it just needs more substrate to get there (Km up). Non-competitive sabotages the machine from elsewhere — extra substrate cannot help, so the ceiling drops (Vmax down) while binding is unaffected (Km unchanged). Uncompetitive only clamps onto the enzyme once substrate is already bound — it drags both values down together, giving those tell-tale parallel lines.

sections.title: How does the cell keep enzymes in check?

blocks.x: Cells regulate enzyme activity through several strategies working together, all aimed at cellular economy — not wasting resources running the wrong reactions at the wrong time.

Some enzymes have an extra allosteric site beyond the active site. Allosteric modulators bind there: a positive effector at an "activator site" boosts activity, while a negative effector at an "inhibitor site" reduces it. Analogy: like a remote control switch on the side of a machine — you're not touching the main controls, but you can still turn performance up or down from a distance.

Some enzymes are made as inactive proenzymes or zymogens and only become active once specific peptide bonds are irreversibly cut — e.g. chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin, pepsinogen → pepsin, plasminogen → plasmin. Analogy: like a safety pin on a tool that must be physically removed before the tool can be used — a one-way, permanent activation step.

Opposing pathways (like building up vs. breaking down fatty acids or glycogen) are kept running in different cellular compartments, so they don't cancel each other out. Analogy: a construction crew and a demolition crew working out of separate offices in the same company — keeping their work physically apart avoids one team constantly undoing the other's job.

Enzymes aren't immortal — half-lives vary widely, e.g. LDH lasts 5–6 days, while amylase lasts only 3–5 hours. Rate-limiting enzymes often have short half-lives, allowing tight, fast control over how much active enzyme is available at any moment — much like a company adjusting staffing levels quickly by using short-term contracts for its most critical, fast-changing roles.

sections.title: Ribozymes — when RNA does the enzyme's job

blocks.x: Not every catalyst in the cell is a protein. Ribozymes are RNA molecules that function as biological catalysts. In 1983, Altman and coworkers found that ribonuclease P contained an RNA component with genuine enzyme activity — one that even obeys Michaelis-Menten kinetics, just like a protein enzyme. RNA molecules can fold into complex 3D (tertiary) structures, just as proteins do, which is what allows them to catalyze reactions too.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — the manager doing the worker's job

blocks.x: Normally, DNA/RNA "manages" information while proteins "do the work" of catalysis. A ribozyme is like a manager who occasionally rolls up their sleeves and does the hands-on job themselves — proof that the roles aren't as strictly separated as once thought. The Varkud satellite (VS) ribozyme is the largest known nucleolytic (RNA-cutting) ribozyme discovered.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — reading spilled ink to find the broken bottle

blocks.x: When a specific tissue is damaged, its enzymes "spill" into the bloodstream — much like ink leaking from a specific broken bottle tells you which bottle broke, even if you didn't see it happen. Doctors read these enzyme levels in blood tests as clues pointing back to exactly which organ or tissue is in trouble.
Isoenzymes — the same job, different versions

Isoenzymes (isozymes) catalyse the same reaction but are built slightly differently, and are typically characteristic of particular tissues. That tissue-specificity is what makes them so useful clinically: measuring which version is raised tells you where the damage is.

c: Five isoenzymes (LDH-1 to LDH-5), made from H and M subunits in different combinations
LDH-1 is richest in heart and red cells; LDH-5 in liver and skeletal muscle
CK-MB points to heart muscle; CK-MM to skeletal muscle; CK-BB to brain
Liver, bone, placental and intestinal forms
Distinguishes liver disease from bone disease when total ALP is raised

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — same tool, different brands

blocks.x: Think of isoenzymes as the same tool made by different manufacturers: they all do the job, but each workshop stocks its own brand. Find a particular brand lying somewhere it shouldn't be, and you know exactly which workshop it came from. That is precisely how a raised CK-MB points at the heart rather than at a pulled muscle.

sections.title: Key takeaways

items: Enzymes are biocatalysts (mostly proteins, with RNA ribozymes as a rare exception) that speed up specific reactions without being permanently changed.
Systematic naming sorts every enzyme into one of 6 IUB classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, and ligases.
Only a tiny active site on a much larger protein does the actual catalysis, described by either the rigid lock-and-key model or the flexible induced fit model.
Many enzymes need helper cofactors — loosely-bound coenzymes or tightly-bound prosthetic groups — to become a fully functional holoenzyme.
Activity is shaped by temperature, pH, substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, and exposure to light/radiation.
Inhibitors can be reversible (competitive, non-competitive, uncompetitive, mixed) or irreversible (often toxic, permanent).
Cells fine-tune enzyme activity through allosteric regulation, zymogen activation, compartmentalization, and controlled synthesis/degradation.
Enzymes power real-world applications in medicine, diagnostics, genetics, and industry — and abnormal enzyme levels in blood are key diagnostic clues for disease.

lines: "Oh Trusty Hydrolase, Lyase Isomerase Ligase" — Oxidoreductases, Transferases, Hydrolases, Lyases, Isomerases, Ligases (1-6 in order).
"Competitive = Km Changes" — competitive inhibitors raise the apparent Km (need more substrate to compete), but Vmax stays the same since enough substrate can still out-compete the inhibitor.
"Non-competitive = Vmax Changes" — binds elsewhere, so no amount of extra substrate helps — Vmax drops, Km unchanged.

mnemonics.h: Lock and Key vs Induced Fit
lines: "Lock and Key is rigid, Induced Fit is a handshake" — a handshake reshapes around the other hand, just like induced fit reshapes around the substrate.
Competitive — resembles substrate, binds active site, raises apparent Km, Vmax unchanged
Non-competitive — binds elsewhere, Vmax decreases, Km unchanged
Uncompetitive — binds ES complex only, both Km and Vmax decrease
Induced Fit (Koshland) — active site reshapes around substrate

steps.title: How an Enzyme Catalyzes a Reaction

items.d: The substrate molecule diffuses toward the enzyme's active site.
The active site reshapes slightly around the substrate, forming the enzyme-substrate (ES) complex.
The enzyme lowers the activation energy needed, stabilizing the high-energy transition state.
Bonds are broken/formed; cofactors or coenzymes may participate directly in the chemistry.
The product no longer fits the active site well and is released.
The unchanged enzyme is free to bind a new substrate molecule and repeat the cycle.
